title: Pulled pork
subtitle: Slow-roasted spiced pork shoulder that shreds with a fork
excerpt: Pulled pork is a pork shoulder rubbed with brown sugar, smoked paprika, and spices, then roasted low and slow in a covered pot until the meat collapses and pulls apart in long strands. The oven version takes 6 to 7 hours. Pile it into soft buns with coleslaw and a sharp vinegar sauce.
sourceNotes: American BBQ tradition, particularly associated with the Carolinas, where whole-hog and shoulder smoking is a regional craft. Oven-roasted pulled pork follows the same principles as the pit-smoked original. Background from Edna Lewis, The Taste of Country Cooking (1976), and WPA Carolina food surveys.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze pulled pork with its juices in portions for up to 3 months. Thaw overnight and reheat in a covered pan with a splash of water.
recipe.batchNotes: A large shoulder feeds 8 to 10 people. The cooked meat keeps in the fridge for 4 days and freezes well.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cook the day before: shred while warm, then refrigerate in its juices. The fat solidifies on top overnight and can be lifted off. Reheat gently in a covered pan.

glossaryTerms.definition: The dark, caramelised outer crust that forms on slow-cooked or smoked meat as the surface dries and the spice rub cooks into a firm shell. In pulled pork, the bark is considered the best part.

content.text: Pulled pork is pork shoulder cooked at 150°C for 6 to 7 hours until the collagen has broken down completely and the meat falls apart in long strands. A dry rub of brown sugar, smoked paprika, and spices forms the
on the outside as it cooks. The oven gives a reliable result without a smoker.

Mix together the {{light-brown-sugar}} of brown sugar, {{paprika-smoked}} of smoked paprika, {{sea-salt-flakes}} of salt, {{black-pepper}} of pepper, {{garlic-powder}} of garlic powder, {{onion-powder}} of onion powder, {{cayenne-pepper}} of cayenne, {{cumin-ground}} of cumin, and {{mustard-powder}} of mustard powder. Score the pork shoulder skin in a diamond pattern. Rub the mixture all over the meat. For the best result, leave uncovered in the fridge overnight.
Heat the oven to 150°C. Place the pork in the Dutch oven or a deep roasting tin. Add 200 ml of water to the base. Cover tightly with a lid or foil. Roast for 6 hours.

Remove the lid or foil. Raise the oven to 200°C and roast uncovered for 30 minutes to firm up and darken the bark. The meat is ready when a fork meets no resistance anywhere and the internal temperature is above 90°C.

Rest the pork, covered loosely, for 30 minutes. Pull the meat apart using two forks or your fingers: it should separate easily into long, moist strands. Mix the {{cider-vinegar}} of vinegar and {{ketchup}} of ketchup with the pan juices to make a quick finishing sauce. Toss the pulled pork with the sauce and serve in buns.

items.cause: Oven too cool, or a particularly large joint.
items.fix: Cook for another hour. Pulled pork is done when the bone (if present) pulls out cleanly and a fork twists through the meat with no resistance.

items.cause: Lid left on throughout without the uncovered finish.
items.fix: The uncovered 30-minute blast at 200°C is what sets and darkens the bark. Do not skip this step.

items.cause: Boneless shoulder cooked without liquid, or cooking temperature too high.
items.fix: Boneless shoulder dries faster than bone-in. Keep the liquid in the base and check at 5 hours.

content.text: Carolina pulled pork uses an Eastern Carolina vinegar sauce: equal parts cider vinegar and water, salt, pepper, and chilli flakes, with no ketchup. Serve with a separate Carolina mustard sauce (yellow mustard, vinegar, brown sugar) for the South Carolina style. Slow cooker pulled pork works well: 8 hours on low with the dry-rubbed joint and 100 ml of apple juice.

Pulled pork is central to American BBQ culture, above all in the Carolinas, where whole-hog barbecue is a centuries-old tradition at community gatherings and church events. The oven version makes it accessible year-round. The key is time: nothing substitutes for the hours the meat needs to break down.
